posts.caption:
Mudang primarily work with a pantheon of 신 shin we usually refer to as our 신령님 shinryungnim. It's our shinryungnim who open the doors to various abilities, specialities, and types of rituals and ceremonies we can do as mudang

Our shinryungnim can be a mix of celestials, deities, bodhisattvas, saints and other types of gods, in addition to, our own defied ancestors. This is a big part of why what one mudang does might not work for another mudang, and won't work for those who are not initiated mudang. Central to our practices is our relationship with our own unique pantheon that no other mudang has

We also work with gods outside of our own pantheon when that is required to help our clients

At the end of the day, being a mudang is a closed practice. It's a tradition that is embodied through the historical traditions that were found on the Korean peninsula, but the core of mudang lineages is from the spirits

Ancestors do not select the mudang, the gods do. We in turn, have a responsibility to care for the world and all sentient beings. That often requires a mix of oral traditions passed down to us through our lineage elders, adaptation and resourcefulness in the face of an ever changing world, and inspiration from our shinryungnim 

It's an immense responsibility, and we aren't picked because we are "perfect." Being a mudang necessitates that we are human first. There is no mudang who is not human, and the more fully we embrace our humanity, the better healers and guides we become

The feminine is always part of the masculine, and the masculine is always part of the feminine. You see, they were never separate to begin with, but elements of a whole. We need both, regardless of how we identify. A healthy relationship with both energies is important

Trans, non-binary, agender, femme, masc, woman, man... No matter how you identify, every person has what we understand as feminine and masculine energies, and we need them both for spiritual balance. We become stiff and fragile when our energies are not allowed to be dynamic and in harmony 

Feminine is not always saying "yes", and never saying "no" 

Feminine is not forcing yourself to smile and be pleasant while you bury your true feelings

Feminine is not shutting down your critical thinking 

To be clear, these things are not masculine either

I started the energetic year of the Fire Horse working with fire in ritual. I was reminded that fire burns what is flammable. Period. 

Fire demands respect, awareness and one who is willing to listen

A big portion of the files have been released--and though this event takes on a triumphant tone for many, it should be sobering, too 

We are reminded once again, that victims and survivors in the U.S. are rarely centered. Their information and stories disrespected, even in the process of seeking truth and justice 

We are all burning 

As a SA survivor, the entire process leading up to the files being dropped has been wrought with many thoughts and emotions. I too, felt triumph at the news that the files had dropped. I also felt pain 

I felt worry for those who may be retraumatized or triggered in various ways by the continuing influx of SA and human trafficking content flooding their feeds and news. If you are, please take time for yourself. As much time as you need. Making content can wait. Reading the files can wait (indefinitely). That is the most revolutionary thing you can do for yourself. In a system that constantly cuts and inflicts trauma based on a time table, please heal. Don't rush. Take your time. Do what you need to do to be present. Set and maintain boundaries. Surround yourself with those that help you process, when you are able to. Community should ground you in lived reality. Your existence and its reality matters 

For those who may not be able to empathize with survivors, I humbly ask you to consider our realities before you speak on the files. Ending cycles does not mean erasing a circle entirely, but rather, breaking a circle so that it can spiral into a different plane from 2D to 3D. Often, well meaning words can inflict the same traumas and perpetuate the very cycles they mean to break. They can end up erasing one circle only to unknowingly copy and paste it elsewhere, instead of transforming it. So please speak, but be wise. I believe in you

A blaze will burn everyone indiscriminately

posts.caption:
With Korea being in the northern hemisphere, this day is observed as the winter solstice. On 동짓날 Dongji, it’s traditional to make 팥죽 red bean porridge. The red bean porridge is first served to the gods of the home, the ancestors, and then to the living who reside at the home 

Another tradition is to fling red bean porridge outside the home or to smear it by the entrances, as it’s thought this will scare away lowly spirits during the long night of the winter solstice. Alternatively if you don’t have red bean porridge you can throw plain red beans or put bowls of red beans at places you would have smeared porridge on (like by your front door) 

The winter solstice marks the turn of the season from autumn to winter, metal to water, Sagittarius to Capricorn. It’s a day naturally dominated by yin energy, and a good time to move slowly and gently. Finding the path of least resistance and flowing like water, rather than blasting through moments with intensity and vigor

Happy Dongji! May you find rest in the darkness and warmth by the fire 🕯️

posts.caption:
Winter solstice is called dongji 동짓날 in Korean. It was regarded as the beginning of the year long ago. We also have January 1st, Ipchun 입춘, and Seollal/Korean New Year 설날. Each one having been regarded as some kind of beginning — a new year — at some point in time

These days can serve as a time for endings, beginnings, as a doorway, times of new or renewed momentum, and so on…

Connecting to ancestral traditions looks different for everyone. If you’ve ever felt invited to observe one of these days more than the others, it could be a nudge from the ancestors you have the strongest connection to

Alternatively, perhaps you feel nudged to observe traditions on January 1st, even though it’s not “traditional.” This could be your ancestors encouraging you to adapt. It’s a good reminder that traditions can be observed in many ways, and what’s practical for us as their descendants should be taken into consideration too

For those in the northern hemisphere, winter solstice is quickly approaching this weekend, while the summer solstice is quickly approaching for our friends in the southern hemisphere. However you spend the solstice, may it be everything you need for the year ahead!✨

✨What Do Mudang Do?✨ 

Our main purpose is to help beings, including human beings! 

That can come in the form of blessings and protection for children, undoing knots and twists of fate/course correction, blessings for the success of businesses, helping ghosts pass on to the afterlife, providing spiritual consultation for life matters, one year life forecast readings, general divination and prophecy, banishing lowly spirts from houses, exorcisms, blessing movie sets, making protective and empowering amulets for athletes and fighters, etc. 

The mudang tradition is an indigenous folk tradition. We adapt to situations and make adjustments as we go. What we do involves thinking quickly on our feet. This is  a big reason why an apprenticeship period is necessary for mudang. Even for quick-learners, there really is no substitute for the invaluable lessons of time and experience

posts.caption:
✨Mudang & Korean culture✨

Mudang have been shaped by, and have helped shape, Korean culture for thousands of years. A semi-traditional or hyper-traditional lineage mudang ceremony (굿) may give people a glimpse into parts of Korean culture that have faded away in mainstream culture (specific elements of clothing, symbols, colors, etc.)

At the same time, mudang traditions are very much their own thing. Let me explain…

We may use traditional instruments like 장구 janggu and 징 jjing, but we play them in a music style that is specific to mudang music

You might see traditional Korean symbols of certain flowers and animals on our clothing, both they may hold a slightly different meaning for mudang

We may use Korean as our main language of worship, but even the use of certain words in a mudang context differs from how they would be used otherwise

So, although our traditions are Korean, they’re specifically Korean in a mudang way

You won’t find details about our traditions in books because it’s a closed practice. Scholarly research tries its best to describe our traditions with what information is available to them, but it’s always good to remember the value of consulting an actual mudang if you have questions about what we do 😊

________

✨Mudang work with all kinds of spirits✨

We have a pantheon of deities we serve at our personal shrines. These are the gods — that include deified ancestors — who are the source of our abilities and talents as mudang

We often work with the ancestors of our clients too. Whether it’s relaying direct messages to their descendants, or working with them to help our clients, ancestors are high on the list of spirits we work with!

Mudang are intimately tied to nature and the land, so we also tend to work with the spirts of the land that we’re on. This does not mean we work with spirits that are from other closed traditions (Ex. Native closed practice deities), but that we interact with the local spirits in a respectful way

posts.caption:
Families can be complex. Ancestors can be complex. 

Being mixed is something that was looked down upon for a myriad of reasons, and it’s not surprising. When existence is political, the existence of mixing can seem threatening. One may wonder, where are the boundaries and “rules” that kept identities separate and tidy? 

…But would it be so radical to sit with the discomfort first, rather than acting out on what triggered discomfort? 

Would it be so radical to lean into someone’s identity and humanity, rather than how their existence threatens your comfort? 

It takes a lot of individual and collaborative work to heal past cycles and make sure wisdom continues to be transmitted through the generations

It can feel impossible at times to push through. Like we have too much on our plate, but can’t figure out what to do

Do we find a bigger plate? Maybe we should just find a huge tray? Do we eat faster? Do we invite more people to eat with us? Should we cut off the source of food? Is that possible? 

[And perhaps I love food, which is how we find ourselves with this analogy 😆]

All this to say… There is a way. It’s not often going to be easy with families and ancestors. It’s going to look different for everyone, but the heart we act with is what matters most

posts.caption:
I used to be a competitive dancer when I was younger. We’d go over our scores after competitions and there would always be one judge who was on the voice tape. We would play their tapes and listen to their critiques as a team

One time, we were listening to the tape when the judge pointed out a dancer (it was me). They told me to “open my eyes.”

Watching YouTube make-up tutorials as a teen, I quickly realized none of them were made by people that looked like me. Even the asian ones. Everyone had distinct double eyelids and bigger eyes, while I basically had no fold/crease and small eyes (this was in the early 2000s) 

It took me a few years to appreciate my own eyes. A lot of my peers who shared similar eyes ended up getting surgery, or using double eyelid glue or tape to achieve the double eyelid look. I tried the tape once and quickly realized I didn’t like it on myself. I didn’t look like ME 

So, even though I didn’t like how others felt about my eyes (and I couldn’t figure out how I wanted to wear eyeliner for a while 😆), I kept my eyes just the way they were

One day, well into my 20s, I looked in the mirror and realized how much I’d grown to love my eyes. It wasn’t just acceptance, but I really embraced and appreciated them. Somewhere along the way, I’d stopped caring what others thought about them, and that allowed me to love myself without disruption

If there’s parts of you that you love, but feel pressured to change because of what others think and say, LOVE YOURSELF ANYWAYS. Don’t let other people ruin the love you could be showing to yourself 🫰🏻

Some more photos from the Chuseok festivities!

House gods and ancestors are all spirits that lay people in Mugyo can work with! In the first photo, I’m offering a humble Chuseok spread to a house god called “성주 sungju” 

In the second photo, I’m 음복 fevering the offerings that had been made to the ancestors during our Chuseok 차례 charye (ancestral rite). The offering spread had included various dishes including 송편 songpyeon, 전 jjun, 나물 namul and 토란국 toranguk

In Korean, we technically don’t say we “work” with gods or ancestors. We say “모신다” [mo-shin-da]. This means we keep someone we respect or hold in high esteem close to us, caring for them and serving them. This emphasizes our relationship with gods and ancestors, rather than obligation or transactional exchanges

posts.caption:
There’s nothing wrong with changing paths

Some have a path that entails they’ll be dedicated to a single practice, religion, or philosophy their whole lives. Others may never feel drawn to make any of these aforementioned things a big part of their lives. There’s also those who might find themselves switching over to a different framework of practice after having dedicated years of their life to the study and practice of another

Converting or finding out that we’re called to walk a different path years down the line doesn’t mean that we messed up by not choosing the right path the first time. Sometimes it’s just about timing 

It’s okay to honor the communities, spirits and practice that gave us so many experiences and lessons, even if we’re no longer practicing the religion 

Just because a religion, spiritual practice or lineage isn’t right for us at this time, it doesn’t mean it does not hold value for anyone else. In fact, it can still hold value for us after we’ve stopped practicing it, just in a different way than when we were directly involved

The practice we leave behind doesn’t have to be labeled “bad” or “wrong” and the new practice we go into doesn’t have to be “right” or “better than”

Many things can be true all at once. Sometimes a big shift in our path just means we’re being asked to make room for more of the truth 

I’ve been there, and I still often think back to the years before I was a mudang. There’s been times I just needed to sit with anger, disappointment or just flat out confusion as to why things are the way they are, and that’s okay

It’s okay to allow yourself time to process and go through the different thoughts and feelings that can come-up while going through big changes. These moments of processing might come in long seasons or as brief moments that are sprinkled throughout the years 

There might be a time  when you can look back in gratitude. A time when lessons learned in the past seemingly continue into the present in their own magical way. A time when things develop and reveal themselves in ways you never could have understood before

posts.caption:
Another term I should mention is “aedong jaeja” or “aedong” for short. This is what some might translate into English as baby mudang 😊

Aedong jaeja 애동제자 is what I am. It’s a term used to refer to young disciples who are still in the formation and development stages of learning lineage traditions

The aedong phase starts once we’re initiated, and is a critical time of learning. Aedong spend a lot of time with our spirit parent/god parent who will prepare us to become independent full fledged mudang 

Though there may be spirit-led elements of our tradition, we also have wisdom and teachings that have been passed down through the centuries. These teachings are a significant part of our practices and take time to learn well

How long someone is an aedong can really vary. It’s a little different than going to school and finishing a program within a pre-determined time frame. It’s more about determining when we are ready

At minimum, we can be considered aedong for 3-5 years. Of course, the learning never stops and will continue for the rest of our lives, but becoming a full fledged mudang means we should have built a strong foundation to our practice, and are able to make decisions independently without needing guidance from our spirit parent

posts.caption:
An ancestral rite I had the honor of doing for a client’s ancestors 🙏🏻

For those who have been asking how to do ancestral veneration in the Korean style, I’ve got something in the works for you. Stay tuned for that! 

Chuseok 추석/Hangawi 한가위/Mid-Autumn Festival is coming up on October 6th. This is one of the special days when we prepare a bigger ancestral offering called charye 차례(similar to what’s pictured here) 

Though there are plenty of regional and family specific variations, one of the staple offerings for ancestral rites is called three-colored namul 삼색나물. The three symbolic colors of this dish are brown, white and green 

My family traditionally used spinach 시금치, balloon flower root 도라지 and fern bracken 고사리 for the three colors. I’ve also heard of other families using other kinds of namul instead 

Ancestral veneration is a time of remembering and honoring the wisdom of those who came before us. It can also be a time to reflect on mistakes and generational cycles that we’d like to intentionally address and meaningfully change moving forward

Well, for one, the experience of being Korean (or any other identity), is not to be overgeneralized. Every single person who identifies as Korean is entitled to their own opinions. posts.caption:
I grew up in the aftermath of the LA Riots. My early experiences left me with more questions than answers. Perhaps some of you have had a similar experience? 

When I was around 9 years old, I climbed up into a tree with two other friends. We settled into the trees wide branches and talked excitedly in Korean when two neighborhood kids ran to the base of the tree and began yelling, “Ching Chong” remarks at us. They threw sticks and stones at us, one of which, landed and cut my eyelid. An elder family member who had lost their shop in the LA Riots happened to be home that day. When I returned home, they noticed my eye immediately and ran out to find the neighborhood kids who had hurt me. Back then, I didn’t know how to say it, but I knew part of my hesitancy in telling my family member what had happened, was because the kids who had thrown sticks and stones were brown and black. I knew my family member could be very discriminatory towards other POC, particularly blacks. The scars of the LA Riots ran deep for them. I knew that for them, the intent was to protect, but I couldn’t help but feel there was a better way

Fast forward to just about a week ago. I briefly stopped by a popular sandwich spot on the way to work. I needed some extra fuel and this spot sold really strong coffee. When I walked in, there was a young black man who looked like they were waiting for an order. I stood by the cash register waiting to order. The cashier walked out a few moments later calling out a to-go order and its details. This order was for the young man. He stayed silent for a while and then began to call the cashier racist for getting his order wrong when they never get orders wrong when the customer is yt. The cashier was perplexed. They were Asian. When the young man left, the cashier later pondered out loud to their co-worker how they could be racist when they too, are a minority and POC, and had tried their best to fulfill the order 

I share both of these stories to say, Asian communities are still wrestling with the tension between us and other POC groups. This discussion is relevant and will continue to be

(자동)차 고사 cha gosa AKA car spirit blessing 

This is something anyone can do for their cars or vehicles. During a gosa, you make offerings to the spirit of your vehicle. You pray they will keep you and your passengers safe and out of danger, and wish the spirit a long healthy life 

If a mudang does the gosa for you, you can expect their gods will be blessing your vehicle as well! They may also provide talismans to keep with the car after the gosa 

What offerings are made and how a gosa is done can vary depending on lineage and region, but here are some general tips if you’d like to try for yourself as a lay person…

Offer fresh water, bottle of soju or makgeolli, fruits, 씨루덕 red bean rice cake, and 북어포 dried fish 

Place offerings in front of the car and greet the spirit by bowing. Pray, and then circle the vehicle as you pour the soju on the ground around the vehicle 

You can pour the water on the vehicle gently and sprinkle some of it on the interior of your vehicle too

The offerings are considered blessed and you can eat them after the gosa 

It’s recommended you do a gosa for your vehicle when you first get it, or if it starts having issues

But what about other spirits? Lowly spirits that want to attach to us, stronger heavy spirits who love tricking us and causing all manner of mischief, both acute and chronic? What about all the other kinds of spirits that exist in this world and influence our lives in their own ways? 

Essentially, there are always going to be spirits that do not share the same goals as us, and have different priorities than we do. This is life. C’est la vie~ This is how it is with other humans, as well. Right?

So, rather than getting wrapped up in fear, frustration or rigid and dichotomous judgments, especially when interacting with spirits that may test my own goals (or even threaten my own goals), I choose to take the interaction as a potential learning lesson

So what if they try to trick me? I can play the game and I will always play well as long as I stay true to my purpose in this world. It’s possible to trick a trickster, and gain much insight through that process

Candle blooms are auspicious ✨ 

Candle blooms 촛불꽃 happen when the very top of the wick blossoms into the shape of a flower(s) while lit. Candle blooms come in many different shapes and sizes, and can vary in exact meaning. They’re usually personal messages from 신령님 our gods to us. They can also happen on ancestral altars or any other setting where spirits are communicating to us through a burning candle

When candles bloom, the way the length of the exposed wick + tip of the wick are shaped are typically much more delicate than when a wick mushrooms (which can often happen when a candle burns poorly). Candle mushrooms are usually very bulky and need to be trimmed off

Candle blooms fall off on their own, and leave behind a delicate stem. They can bloom on occasion, or bloom repeatedly one after the other on the same candle. The exactly meaning is usually personal to you and your spirits, so discern for yourself what may be being communicated to you if your shrine or altar candles bloom! 

The first candle bloom I saw after my 신내림굿 initiation was shaped like a beautiful orchid (no, I don’t have photos. I don’t take photos of everything, you know?😆) My gods affirmed my path and encouraged me to work towards certain things that were developing at the time

✨Shrine of 1,000 Helping Hands✨

The name of the shrine came about through months of prayer and intentional thought. In Korean hangul the shrine name is written 천아동 신당 (chun ahdong shindang), and is primarily written in hanja/Sino-Korean as 天兒童神堂. The secondary hanja is 千兒童神堂. These two hanja versions of the shrine name are pronounced the same and written the same in hangul, and serve to express a double meaning. The primary name means “Shrine of the Celestial Children” while the secondary name means “Shrine of 1,000 Children.” Fitting titles for a shrine whose tiny and powerful child gods bring so much joy, blessings and protection to the people they help 👼🏻👼🏻👼🏻

In English, Shrine of 1,000 Helping Hands serves as a translation of  the shrine’s Korean name and its reference to the many child gods present in the pantheon. It also makes reference to the 1,000 arms of Guan Shi Yin 관세음보살 that compassionately come to the aid of many. Known as Guanyin to most, this beloved bodhisattva resides at the Shrine of 1,000 Helping Hands as well, alongside many other gods who make it possible for many to be helped

Though there are limitless many who need aid, I will strive to help them all 
Though there are endless lessons of truth to learn, I will continue learning them all

With each passing year, I’ll continue to dedicate myself to cultivation and study. I may make mistakes, but I won’t make them in vain. With the help of my gods and my community I will grow stronger and more focused so I can help more and more people! 

The Shrine of 1,000 Helping Hands will grow and I pray it will be a safe haven for many throughout the years

posts.caption:
Samjae 삼재 can be translated as “the three calamities”

Samjae is a period of 3 consecutive years that are said to bring misfortune into one’s life. To try and mitigate the effects of their samjae, people buy talismans specifically made for this purpose, and have rituals called samjae puri 삼재풀이 done at buddhist temples or by mudangs

Before you freak out, hear me out! The samjae energies interact with every individual’s fate lines a little differently. This can mean that sometimes the calamities are tiny and not very noticeable. Other samjae cycles may leave you feeling absolutely defeated. Other cycles you may actually enjoy some good fortune instead of calamities. This last one would be called boksamjae 복삼재 

For myself, I’m in my last year of samjae and it was not boksamjae this cycle 💀 So, rituals and chants were done to mitigate many misfortunes

2022, 2023, 2024 were the samjae years for those born in the years of the rat, dragon & monkey. For anyone whose with me in this cycle, our samjae will be over with the start of the lunar new year on January 29, 2025 👏

2025 will mark the beginning of samjae for those born in the years of the rabbit, sheep & pig! If that’s you, take care in 2025, 2026 and 2027. You can always have a session with a mudang to see how this samjae cycle will affect you. Some people get samjaepuri done as soon as they can, while others wait to get it done once they run into trouble. The lucky ones won’t have to worry because it’s boksamjae for them 😆

Sometimes we think we must look upwards to find the gods and devas, but this isn’t always so. As I sat at the jesa table I had prepared for my late grandmother, we had a conversation. One that helped me see the generational patterns and trauma that linked us together. As she revealed these things to me, I was so thankful to have shared this time with her. At the same time, my heart ached for her. For all the pain she endured and persevered through. The grief and disappointment that she had not had the proper opportunity to air while alive. Our farewell was sweet and warm. She reassured me she was well taken care of, and that she would not need jesa in the future. The Catholic offerings and prayers of my parents were enough for her. Still, we enjoyed the short time we had together as she enjoyed the jesa table I had set for her for the first and last time

Jesa is an ancestral ritual that takes place on either the night before your ancestor’s death anniversary, or on the actual day of their death anniversary. It’s an opportunity to connect with a loved one who has passed on, and to provide for them while they work through the afterlife

Traditionally, a family would have separate dish ware for these ancestral rites. Up until now, I’ve just been using what I have, hoping that one day I’ll be able to buy my ancestors nice serving wares. Then, recently I was given our family set of jesa dish wares. I was not even aware we had any. I was shocked, but I could feel my ancestors brimming with excitement. At last, proper dish wares. At last I’d figured out where to find them

As I washed each bowl and lid, I was filled with joy and excitement. Gratitude came in waves as well. What a beautiful life I have. A life where my family ties are mending before my eyes, and I’m being helped along by my gods and ancestors. These may just look like metal bowls, but to me, they’re a gift from my gods. They’re a gift from my ancestors. It’s a message that I’m on the right track and that my gods will provide for me and those I love

I’m really looking forward to using these dishes for the next family jesa. I know my ancestors are looking forward to it as well 🙂🙏🏻

“How do you learn how to be a mudang?“

My thesis work had to do with Korean-American Catholics and suggested the significance of food culture in spirituality. Of course I had to do some background research on Korean spirituality, and that was when I found out about “Korean Shamanism”

I had been raised without a mention of it until my mid-20s, when I kept reading about this “Korean Shamanism” that played such a significant role in the spirituality of the Korean people. 

All of the sources I read were written by academics and scholars. None were written by Korean shamans. A majority were written from an ethnographic or theatrical/performative perspective. 

Many of the articles felt like recycled information I had read in other articles. There was usually some mention of the gut ritual 굿, shinbyeong 신병, initiation 신내림굿, and the stigma associated with mudang 무당. 

Fast forward many years after writing my thesis, and I’m now an initiated apprentice. I’ve realized how much more there is to Korean Shamanism AKA mugyo 무교

There are so many more kinds of rituals and workings that we do beyond the gut ritual. There are so many different styles/ lineages of mudangs. Stigma is also such a nuanced thing rooted in a specific cultural and social context. I’m finding out what that means, or doesn’t mean for me day-by-day as Korean diaspora. 

How do you learn how to be a mudang? 

Before anything else, you need to confirm you have a calling to be a mudang by being vetted by an elder shaman. Sometimes this can mean being vetted by elders of traditions outside of mugyo (if you do not have access to mudang elders). This is especially true for the Korean diaspora populations. Then you find the right spirit mentor who will initiate you into their lineage.

I learn tradition that is specific to the lineage I was initiated into through my spirit mentor. These traditions are only passed down to initiated spirit family members. Then there are the lessons I learn directly from my shin 신령님 AKA gods.

Following initiation, it is through tradition & spirit family, our shin, constant effort, and time that we learn how to be mudang.

Cute pic? Kind of. Here’s the story… 

I was running around, trying to help prepare things for 굿 grand ceremony. I was tired and a little overwhelmed, but I was really pushing to learn as much as I could throughout the prep. 

When I went to change out of my 한복 hanbok, I noticed the  butterflies at the bottom of my skirt were gone. My mental processing speed was very low from lack of sleep, but it finally hit me after a few seconds— my skirt was inside out 🫠

It had been inside-out the WHOLE time. Before, during and after 굿 grand ceremony. It’s little humbling moments like this when I realize (1) it’s time to check-in with myself and (2) get some rest. Also, ended up not being a big deal because it looked fine, but it was just funny finding out AFTER we had been in ceremony for hours 🤣

So anyways, my skirt is inside-out in this photo. Thanks for taking a nice photo of us @that.korean.witch 🫰🏻

Humble offering this new moon 초하루. Sweet potato leaves and loquats from the garden, and assorted goodies from the grocery store and Mayday Faire this past weekend. 

As a child, I prayed a lot. In my own humble, small way. When I’d be in unbearable pain, in a hopeless situation, or harassed by frightening spirits, I would pray. I would pray sincerely and from the heart. I didn’t know how to ask people for help, but I would pray to the divine to come to my aid. 

As I got older, my relationship changed with prayer. I began to prioritize logic and action. I wondered what good prayers were if they did not move us into action. I wanted to be the change. I wanted to be prayer in action. 

Now, as I continue to reflect and process world events and history, I find myself needing prayer again. No action seems like it’s enough in light of so many genocides we have committed, witnessed, and suffered as a collective. 

So I light candles, make offerings and pray. I pray that we will learn from our mistakes so as not to repeat them. I pray for suffering to be meaningful when it does happen. I pray we’ll do better with every passing generation. 

I pray with words spoken and words offered silently in my heart. 

I prayed, I pray and I am praying.

posts.caption:
There are so many celebrations in the month of May! Cinco de Mayo, Mother’s Day, Pentecost, Asian American and Pacific Islander Heritage Month, and the Month of Mother Mary. There’s so much life buzzing throughout the land in May 🪻🦋🐝🐞🐿️

This year in California, there has been so much rain and the land has really come to life. There are so many flowers blooming everywhere—even in the dessert! Just as the land is moving and growing, I feel called to do the same. 

This May, I feel called to preserve old traditions and to create new ones. 

As an Asian American born and raised in California, I had access to a Korean specific grocery store early on in childhood, rather than having to go to the general Asian or Oriental Markets. I had people around me I could speak Korean to, and a tiny local VHS rental shop that had Korean cartoons that I could watch and learn Korean from. Growing up surrounded by Korean in a land an ocean away from where my ancestors had lived, was certainly a blessing and a privilege. 

Being surrounded by all of it, remembering and recording skills I had learned or stories I’d been told were not high on my priority list. 

Now, my grandparents have all passed on, and I realize how significant their traditions have been as I develop my own traditions. 

Here I am today, on a road that no one would have guessed I would take all those years ago. A mudang apprentice learning the old ways and learning new ways. All the clouds and rain from past years have brought me so many flowers that I can enjoy and cherish in my life.

I’m really looking forward to the month of May, and honoring old traditions, as well as, forging my own path and creating new traditions. 

What are you most looking forward to this May?

I was gifted my first 도장 stamp as a 무당 mudang. I’m grateful for all the people in my life who support me and the path I’ve chosen. Through gifts, their time and energy, words of wisdom, and in other ways, I’m lucky to have people in my corner who accept me and this unconventional life I lead. 

Someone asked me if becoming a mudang had led me to reconnecting to my Korean heritage. I realized it had not, because this need to honor my roots started years ago. I spent my whole life being in the grey areas and the in-between. Neither here nor there, yet still here and there. My heritage is complicated and it’s more than Korean. It’s also Japanese. It’s more than just Seoul (though I speak 서울말 Seoul dialect), it’s 황해도 Hwanghae, 전라도 Jeolla, 경상남도 Gyeongsangnam, 오사카 Osaka. Not to mention I was born and raised in the U.S. 

Becoming a mudang hasn’t led me to reconnecting to my Korean heritage. 

I’m not Korean. I’m not Japanese. I’m not American. Yet, I am all of those things and more. I have my own path to walk that requires me to know who I am and why I am.  Most importantly, I need to forge my own path and continue to grow into who I need to be. 

Becoming a mudang hasn’t led me to reconnecting to my Korean heritage, but it has shown me that I’m not alone. 

It has shown me we don’t always have to walk alone in our respective paths. We need only look up and around us to see that there are many others on their own unique journeys of becoming. There is power in connecting to our roots, and then there is the power of stepping into who we are. They go hand in hand. Everyday as a baby mudang 애동제자, I take steps towards becoming who I am and building my own legacy.

One god, amongst a vast number of gods a mudang can have in their pantheon, is 대신 할머니 or the Great Spirit Grandmother. 

If a Korean shaman-priest has this god in their pantheon, the Great Spirit Grandmother may help them with clients, or provide counsel on shaman responsibilities. 

Our path as mudangs and baksu-mudangs is not easy, but we are blessed to have our gods who guide us and hold us accountable 🙏🏻
